name: Magnesium deodorant
lead: Magnesium deodorant refers to aluminium-free deodorants that use a magnesium compound, most often magnesium hydroxide (the active in milk of magnesia), applied to the underarms to reduce odour.[1][2] Wikipedia's deodorant article notes that milk of magnesia is sometimes used this way, and that some versions contain trace sodium hypochlorite, a bactericide.[1]

Magnesium hydroxide is a poorly soluble white solid used mainly as an antacid and, at higher oral doses, an osmotic laxative.[2] Its deodorant use is not well documented in the reference literature: the Wikipedia article on magnesium hydroxide lists it as an antiperspirant component with no supporting citation.[2]
No clinical studies of magnesium deodorants were found.

paras: Products are sold as creams, sprays or pastes. Proponents present them as an alternative to aluminium-based antiperspirants and to baking soda deodorants, which can be irritating to some users.[1]

Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)2, is produced industrially from seawater and is nearly insoluble in water.[2] Deodorants act on odour rather than sweat; body odour arises from bacterial breakdown of apocrine sweat secretions.[3] Magnesium products are generally described as mildly alkaline and odour-reducing, but no source describing a verified mechanism was located.

Magnesium hydroxide carries a GHS warning for skin, eye and respiratory irritation.[2] Taken orally in large amounts it can cause diarrhoea, and long-term use may theoretically cause hypermagnesemia in kidney failure.[2] These warnings concern the bulk compound and oral use, not topical deodorants.

card.summary: An aluminium-free deodorant using magnesium hydroxide; popular as a natural alternative, but no trials exist.
card.note: No clinical studies; does not reduce sweat.

quick.overview:
Magnesium deodorants use magnesium hydroxide, the ingredient in milk of magnesia, as an aluminium-free way to manage underarm odour.

No published trials were found, and reference sources only briefly mention the use.
quick.mechanism: They act on odour, not sweating. Odour comes from bacteria breaking down apocrine sweat; magnesium products are generally described as mildly alkaline odour reducers.
quick.risks: Magnesium hydroxide is labelled as a mild skin, eye and respiratory irritant in bulk. Oral overuse can cause diarrhoea. No product-specific safety studies were found.
